title: The Enron short-seller warning of AI's debt trap
key_facts: Jim Chanos, the short seller who bet against Enron, told The Observer that debt-financed AI infrastructure could become a systemic risk to the financial system by 2028
He is betting against most "neoclouds" (smaller firms renting out AI computing, such as CoreWeave, Nebius, TeraWulf), calling them highly leveraged landlords valued as tech growth stocks

The Bank of England warned this week of a possible "sharp correction" from AI-related debt issuance; Goldman Sachs counts nearly $200bn of hyperscaler debt bought this year with more than $1tn planned
SoftBank last week raised more than $11bn in the largest junk bond sale in history to invest in OpenAI; Meta and Amazon are using off-balance-sheet vehicles for data centres and chips
Anthropic's leaked prospectus (Reuters) shows 47 percent of sales via Amazon and Google clouds and a Broadcom loan of up to $42bn; Nvidia says circular-financing claims are "ridiculous"
Only 2.2 percent of US households pay for an AI subscription (PNC data); Bain estimates AI infrastructure spending could reach $1.5tn a year by 2031
quote_evidence: "It's really quite unprecedented," said Chanos. "The only thing we found that was bigger was the Chinese real estate bubble from 2010 to 2020."
"[The risk] is not systemic, but at the rate it's going, it probably will be by 2028."
This week the Bank of England warned of the risks of a "sharp correction" due to the "rapid increase in artificial-intelligence-related debt issuance".
why_it_matters_hint: A famous bear and the Bank of England now share a worry: AI is being built on debt that only pays if revenue grows about 45 percent a year
notes: The Observer's own interview; short sellers have a financial interest in talking AI down, which the article itself notes.
